score.formula: A marker in its optimal range scores 100. A marker in watch scores 60. A marker in risk scores 20. A core marker counts two times. Your score is the weighted mean of these points. When the report has fewer than half of the core markers, the highest score is 70. When the report has fewer than a quarter of the core markers, the highest score is 50.

verdict: 3 of 4 markers sit in your calibrated ranges. Anti-TPO antibodies is the one to move first.

moveFirst.reason: Anti-TPO antibodies is 62 IU/mL, above your optimal range of up to 34 IU/mL.

followUps.title: Retest Anti-TPO antibodies in 8 to 12 weeks
followUps.why: Your Anti-TPO antibodies is well outside your calibrated range. A positive value means a higher chance that the thyroid slows over the years. For this reason, TSH is worth checking regularly. Cut-offs differ between test kits, so the lab range is the reference for a borderline value.
followUps.next: Autoimmune thyroid disease raises it, and it is more common in women and after pregnancy. Levels change slowly and do not need repeating often. Book a retest in 8 to 12 weeks. Take both reports to your doctor.

followUps.title: Measure Fasting glucose
followUps.why: Fasting glucose is not on this report. By ADA criteria, 100 to 125 mg/dL is prediabetes, and 126 or above on two tests is diabetes. Catching the rise early gives years to reverse it.
followUps.next: Ask for Fasting glucose at your next blood test. Fasting glucose is the sugar level in your blood after an overnight fast of at least eight hours. It reflects how well the body keeps sugar steady without food.

followUps.title: Measure HbA1c
followUps.why: HbA1c is not on this report. By ADA criteria, 5.7% to 6.4% is prediabetes and 6.5% or above is diabetes. It does not need fasting, which makes it the most practical long-term sugar measure.
followUps.next: Ask for HbA1c at your next blood test. HbA1c is the share of hemoglobin that has sugar stuck to it. Because red cells live about three months, it reflects average sugar over that time.

followUps.title: Measure Fasting insulin
followUps.why: Fasting insulin is not on this report. High fasting insulin with normal sugar is an early sign of insulin resistance, often years before prediabetes. Combined with glucose it gives HOMA-IR.
followUps.next: Ask for Fasting insulin at your next blood test. Insulin is the hormone that moves sugar from blood into cells. Fasting insulin shows how hard the pancreas works to hold fasting sugar in range.

followUps.title: Measure LDL cholesterol
followUps.why: LDL cholesterol is not on this report. LDL is the best-proven cause of heart attack and stroke, and lower is better for arteries. ATP III calls under 100 mg/dL optimal and 160 or above high.
followUps.next: Ask for LDL cholesterol at your next blood test. LDL cholesterol is the cholesterol that low-density lipoprotein particles carry. These particles can lodge in artery walls and build plaque.

followUps.title: Measure HDL cholesterol
followUps.why: HDL cholesterol is not on this report. Low HDL is under 40 mg/dL in men and under 50 in women. It is linked with higher heart risk and insulin resistance. Raising HDL with drugs did not cut heart attacks, so HDL is a signal rather than a target.
followUps.next: Ask for HDL cholesterol at your next blood test. HDL cholesterol is the cholesterol that high-density lipoprotein carries. This lipoprotein returns cholesterol from tissues to the liver. People often call HDL good cholesterol.

followUps.title: Measure Triglycerides
followUps.why: Triglycerides is not on this report. Under 150 mg/dL is normal and 200 or above is high, by ATP III. High triglycerides with low HDL is a typical pattern of insulin resistance and raises heart risk.
followUps.next: Ask for Triglycerides at your next blood test. Triglycerides are fats made from the calories you do not burn right away. They rise after meals, so a fasting test is best.

followUps.title: Measure Apolipoprotein B
followUps.why: Apolipoprotein B is not on this report. ApoB predicts heart risk at least as well as LDL and better when triglycerides are high. ESC/EAS sets under 100 mg/dL for moderate risk, and AHA/ACC treats 130 or above as a risk enhancer.
followUps.next: Ask for Apolipoprotein B at your next blood test. Every LDL, VLDL and Lp(a) particle carries exactly one ApoB protein. Measuring ApoB counts the harmful particles directly.

followUps.title: Measure Lipoprotein(a)
followUps.why: Lipoprotein(a) is not on this report. A high level raises the risk of heart attack, stroke and aortic valve narrowing, even when LDL is good. The EAS calls under 30 mg/dL low and over 50 high.
followUps.next: Ask for Lipoprotein(a) at your next blood test. Lp(a) is an LDL-like particle with an extra protein attached. Your genes mostly set its level, and it stays about the same for life.

followUps.title: Measure High-sensitivity CRP
followUps.why: High-sensitivity CRP is not on this report. The AHA and CDC class under 1 mg/L as low heart risk. They class 1 to 3 as average and above 3 as high. A value above 10 usually reflects a passing infection, so you should repeat the test when you are well.
followUps.next: Ask for High-sensitivity CRP at your next blood test. hs-CRP measures the same protein as CRP but detects much lower levels. That makes it useful for spotting quiet, long-term inflammation.

followUps.title: Measure ALT (SGPT)
followUps.why: ALT (SGPT) is not on this report. ALT is the most liver-specific routine enzyme, and a raised value is often the first sign of fatty liver. The ACG sets the healthy upper limit at 33 U/L for men and 25 for women. This is lower than many lab ranges.
followUps.next: Ask for ALT (SGPT) at your next blood test. ALT is an enzyme made mostly in liver cells. When those cells are inflamed or damaged, ALT leaks into blood.

followUps.title: Measure Creatinine
followUps.why: Creatinine is not on this report. A rising creatinine means the kidneys filter less. Kidney decline is silent until late, so this value is the early warning.
followUps.next: Ask for Creatinine at your next blood test. Creatinine is a waste product of normal muscle activity, and the kidneys clear it from blood. Combined with age and sex it gives the eGFR, the standard estimate of kidney function.

followUps.title: Measure Vitamin D (25-OH)
followUps.why: Vitamin D (25-OH) is not on this report. The Endocrine Society's 2011 guideline calls under 20 ng/mL deficient and 30 or above sufficient. Its 2024 update stopped advising routine testing in healthy adults, but very low levels still harm bone and muscle.
followUps.next: Ask for Vitamin D (25-OH) at your next blood test. This test measures 25-hydroxy vitamin D, the storage form made in the liver from sunlight and food. It reflects supply over the past few weeks.

followUps.title: Measure Vitamin B12
followUps.why: Vitamin B12 is not on this report. Low B12 causes tiredness, tingling, memory problems and large-cell anaemia, and nerve damage can become permanent. The BSH treats under 200 pg/mL as likely deficient and 200 to 300 as a grey zone.
followUps.next: Ask for Vitamin B12 at your next blood test. The body needs vitamin B12 to make red blood cells and to keep nerves healthy. It comes almost only from animal foods such as milk, yogurt (curd), eggs, fish and meat.

followUps.title: Measure Ferritin
followUps.why: Ferritin is not on this report. Low ferritin is the earliest sign of iron deficiency, often before hemoglobin falls. The WHO calls under 15 ng/mL deficient in healthy adults. The AGA uses under 45 to diagnose iron deficiency in anaemia.
followUps.next: Ask for Ferritin at your next blood test. Ferritin is the protein that stores iron inside cells, and a small amount circulates in blood. Its blood level tracks total iron stores.

followUps.title: Measure Hemoglobin
followUps.why: Hemoglobin is not on this report. Low hemoglobin is anaemia, which causes tiredness, breathlessness and poor focus. Very high hemoglobin thickens the blood and is worth a check with a doctor.
followUps.next: Ask for Hemoglobin at your next blood test. Hemoglobin is the iron-rich protein inside red blood cells. It collects oxygen in the lungs and releases it in the tissues. The test measures how much hemoglobin is in a given volume of blood.
